questions.text: (a) Analyse any three reasons responsible for the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

answer.text:
Reasons for the disintegration of the USSR (any three):
(i) Internal weakness of the Soviet system (political and economic) which failed to meet the aspirations of the people.
(ii) Most of the resources were used to maintain and develop the military arsenal, nuclear weapons and space research, which led to a huge burden on the economy of the USSR and the needs of the people got neglected.
(iii) The Soviet system had become stagnant and non-accountable to the people.
(iv) Rampant corruption, inability to correct mistakes, and unwillingness to allow reform made the system unpopular.

questions.text: (a) Analyse any three happenings during Gorbachev’s period that led to the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

answer.text:
Happenings during Gorbachev's period that led to the disintegration of the Soviet Union (any three):
(i) Mikhail Gorbachev, the then General Secretary of the Communist Party, sought to reform the Soviet system. His decision to normalize relations with the West and democratise and reform the Soviet Union had some other effects that neither he nor anyone else intended or anticipated.
(ii) The people of the Soviet bloc started to protest against their own governments and Soviet control. The Soviet Union did not intervene, and the communist regimes collapsed one after another.
(iii) The economic and political reforms initiated by Gorbachev were opposed by leaders within the Communist Party.
(iv) A coup took place in 1991 that was encouraged by Communist Party hardliners. The people had tasted freedom by then and did not want the old-style rule of the Communist Party.
(v) Boris Yeltsin emerged as a national hero in opposing this coup. The Russian Republic, where Yeltsin won a popular election, began to shake off centralised control. Power began to shift from the Soviet centre to the republics.
All these happenings accelerated the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

questions.text: (b) Analyse any three consequences of the disintegration of USSR.

answer.text:
Consequences of the disintegration of USSR (any three):
(i) End of the Cold War.
(ii) End of the ideological conflict between socialist and capitalist countries.
(iii) Power relations in world politics changed.
(iv) The emergence of new independent countries with their own independent aspirations and choices.
(v) Coming up of a unipolar world with the dominance of the US.
(vi) Erstwhile socialist countries turned to capitalism.
(vii) The European Union strengthened itself.
(viii) Some socialist nations got divided.
(ix) The World Bank and IMF started helping the erstwhile republics that adopted democracy.

questions.text: (a) Describe any three factors that make most of the former Soviet Republics prone to conflicts and threats.

answer.text:
Factors that make most of the former Soviet Republics prone to conflicts and threats (any three):
(i) The Soviet system failed to meet the aspirations of the people.
(ii) Economic stagnation for many years.
(iii) The Soviet economy used much of its resources in maintaining a nuclear and military arsenal.
(iv) It had become stagnant in an administrative and political sense.
(v) The rise of nationalism and the desire for sovereignty within various republics.
(vi) Nationalist urges and feelings were very much at work throughout the history of the Soviet Union.
(vii) Ethnic and religious differences within the Central Asian republics, coupled with economic backwardness.
Or any other relevant factor

questions.text: (b) Explain any three reasons that forced Mikhail Gorbachev to initiate reforms in the Soviet Union.

answer.text:
Reasons that forced Mikhail Gorbachev to initiate reforms in the Soviet Union (any three):
(i) Reforms were necessary to keep the USSR abreast of the information and technological revolutions taking place in the West.
(ii) Mikhail Gorbachev also felt the need to normalize relations with the US.
(iii) To reform the Soviet Union economy with the West, the administrative system also forced Gorbachev to initiate reforms in the USSR.
(iv) Reforms were considered essential to liberate the rigid administrative system of the Soviet Union.
(v) Gorbachev felt that the Soviet economy had become stagnant.
(vi) The Communist Party was not accountable to the people; this further created resentment.
(vii) The people in the East European countries which were part of the Soviet bloc started to protest against their own governments and Soviet control.

questions.text: (a) Analyse any three reasons for the disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991.

answer.text:

(ii) Economic stagnation for many years led to consumer shortages.
(iii) The Soviet Union used much of its resources in maintaining nuclear and military arsenals.

questions.text: (b) Analyse any three consequences of Shock Therapy due to which the economies of Second World countries collapsed.

answer.text:

(iii) The value of the Ruble declined and inflation was high.
(iv) The GDP of Russia declined.
(v) Withdrawal of government subsidies pushed people into poverty.
(vi) Academic and intellectual manpower disintegrated or migrated.

questions.text: “The ‘Arab Spring’ was the people’s revolution against injustice.” Support the statement with any two examples.

answer.text:
The Arab Spring was the people's revolution against injustice (any two):
(i) The Arab Spring took root in Tunisia, where the struggle against corruption, unemployment and poverty was started by the public.
(ii) This movement turned into a political movement because people considered the existing problems as an outcome of autocratic dictatorships.
(iii) The demand for democracy that started in Tunisia spread throughout the Muslim-dominated Arab countries of West Asia.
(iv) The regime of Hosni Mubarak in Egypt also collapsed as a result of massive democratic protest.
(v) The influence of the Arab Spring could also be seen in Yemen, Bahrain, Libya and Syria, where similar protests by the people led to democratic awakening throughout the region.

questions.text: Was Shock therapy necessary for making a transition from Socialist economy to Capitalist economy ? Support your answer with two arguments.

answer.text:
Was Shock Therapy necessary for making a transition from Socialist economy to Capitalist economy? (Students can answer in Yes or No; credit for arguments)

For No: European countries may have opted other methods and have given them time to change; European countries should not have exploited their weak position and could have given them justice.

questions.text: (a) Examine any three reasons responsible for the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

answer.text:

questions.text: (b) Examine any three reasons for the friendly and cooperative relations between India and Russia after the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

questions.text: (a) “After the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Indo-Russian relations are gaining new heights.” Support the statement with any four examples.

answer.text:
(a) "After the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Indo-Russian relations are gaining new heights" - four examples:
1. Both share a vision of a multipolar world order.
2. More than 80 bilateral agreements have been signed between India and Russia as part of the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of 2001.
3. India stands to benefit from its relationship with Russia on issues like Kashmir, energy supplies, sharing information on international terrorism, access to Central Asia, and balancing its relations with China.
4. Russia stands to benefit from their relationship because India is the second-largest arms market for Russia.
5. The Indian military gets most of its hardware from Russia.
6. Since India is an oil-importing nation, Russia is important to India and has repeatedly come to the assistance of India during its oil crises.
Or any other relevant point.

questions.text: (b) “After the Second World War, the Soviet Union was considered a superpower of the world.” Support the statement with any four arguments.

answer.text:
(b) "After the Second World War, the Soviet Union was considered a superpower of the world" - four arguments:
1. After the Second World War, the Soviet economy was more developed than the rest of the world, except for the US.
2. It had a complex communication network, vast energy resources including oil, iron and steel machinery production, and a transport sector that connected its remotest areas with efficiency.
3. It had a domestic consumer industry that produced everything from pins to cars.
4. It ensured a minimum standard of living for all citizens, and the government subsidized basic necessities including health, education, childcare and other welfare schemes.
5. There was no unemployment.
6. State ownership was the dominant form of ownership: land and productive assets were owned and controlled by the Soviet State.
Or any other relevant point.

questions.text: (a) Highlight the reasons for the tensions and conflicts faced by any three former Soviet Republics.

answer.text:
(a) Reasons for the tensions and conflicts faced by any three former Soviet Republics:
1. Violation of human rights - in Russia, Chechnya and Dagestan have had violent secessionist movements; Moscow's method of dealing with Chechen rebels and indiscriminate military bombings have led to many human rights violations but failed to deter the aspirations for independence.
2. Civil war - in Central Asia, Tajikistan witnessed a civil war that went on for 10 years till 2001 due to many sectarian conflicts, and in Georgia the demand for independence came from two provinces, resulting in a civil war.
3. Hydrocarbon resources - Central Asia has become a zone of competition between outside powers and oil companies due to vast hydrocarbon resources; for example, China has interest here because of the oil resources, and Chinese have begun to settle around the borders and conduct trade.
Or any other relevant reasons.

questions.text: (b) Highlight any four reasons for the disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991.

answer.text:
(b) Four reasons for the disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991:
1. The Soviet system became very bureaucratic and authoritarian, making life very difficult for its citizens.
2. There was a lack of democracy and absence of freedom of speech, which stifled people who often expressed dissent in jokes and cartoons.
3. The one-party system represented by the Communist Party of the Soviet Union had tight control over all institutions and was unaccountable to the people.
4. The party refused to recognise the urge of people in the 15 different republics that formed the Soviet Union to manage their own affairs, including their cultural affairs.
5. Ordinary people were alienated by slow and stifling administration, rampant corruption, and the inability of the system to correct mistakes it had made.
6. The party bureaucrats gained more privileges than ordinary citizens.
7. People did not identify with the system and with the rulers, and the government increasingly lost popular backing.

questions.text: (a) Analyse any three reasons for the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

answer.text:
(i) It failed to meet the aspirations of the people. The political system became more bureaucratic and freedom of speech was not given there. Rule of one party was not democratic any more.
(ii) USSR spent much of its money on weapons, this led to a huge economic burden. Economic stagnation for many years led to severe consumer shortages. Leaders could not see disparities between this system and the system of the west.
(iii) Gorbachev introduced 'Perestroika' and 'Glasnost' to reform the USSR. But the people were disillusioned when they came to know the realities. Party members felt that they were deprived of their powers and privileges.
(iv) The rise of nationalism and desire for sovereignty within various republics became the most immediate cause for the collapse.
(any three reasons to be analysed)

questions.text: (b) Examine any three consequences of the Shock therapy.

answer.text:
(i) It brought ruin to the economics and disaster upon the people of the entire region.
(ii) Transferring of industries from public to private sector proved to be the virtual disappearance of entire industries. This was called the largest garage sale in history.
(iii) The value of the Ruble declined dramatically and the inflation rate was so high that people lost their savings.
(iv) The withdrawal of government subsidies pushed large sections of the people into poverty.
(v) The collective farm system disintegrated.
(vi) Post-Soviet states, especially Russia, were divided between rich and poor regions resulting in great economic inequality.
(or any other point) (any three consequences with explanation)

questions.text: Highlight any four effects of the shock therapy after the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

questions.text: (a) Why is ‘Shock Therapy’ considered a painful process of transition from an authoritarian socialist system to a democratic capitalist system ? Explain any three reasons.

answer.text:
Shock therapy is considered a painful process of transition as it led to:
(i) A drastic change in the external orientation of these economies. Development was now envisaged through more trade. So it was a switch over to free trade also.
(ii) The large state-controlled industrial complex almost collapsed.
(iii) FDI was considered as an engine of free trade. So these countries had to change their economy based on state ownership and socialist philosophy to a liberal capitalist economy. It was really painful and difficult for the concerned countries.
(iv) It involved a breakup of the existing trade alliances among the countries of the Soviet bloc. Now it was directly related to the west.
(v) The old system of social welfare was systematically destroyed.
(vi) The construction of democratic institutions was not given the same attention and priority as the demands of economic transformation.
(or any other relevant point) (any three) Hence it is considered painful.

questions.text: (b) Explain any four reasons for the disintegration of the Soviet Union.

answer.text:
Reasons for the disintegration of Soviet Union:
(i) Internal weaknesses of the state political and economic institutions.
(ii) Soviet system failed to fulfil the aspirations of the people as it had become corrupt and incompetent.
(iii) The centralisation of authority in a vast land.
(iv) Maintenance of the nuclear and military arsenal and development of satellite programme led to huge economic burden on the people and could not meet the needs and demands of the people.
(v) The Soviet system was not answerable to the people.
(vi) The rise of nationalism and the desire for sovereignty within various republics including Russia and the Baltic Republics.
(vii) Reforms initiated by General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev.
(viii) The ordinary citizens could see the disparities between their system and the system of the west.
(or any other relevant point) (any four)

questions.text: (b) “Despite various problems, the people in all the South Asian countries share the aspiration and support for democracy.” Justify the statement with any three suitable examples.

questions.text: (b) Analyse any three major happenings in Bangladesh that show peoples’ support to democracy.

answer.text:
Major happenings in Bangladesh that show people's support for democracy (any three):
(i) Sheikh Mujibur Rahman led the popular struggle against West Pakistani domination. He demanded autonomy for the eastern region. In the 1970 elections the Awami League won all the seats in East Pakistan, but the government dominated by the West Pakistani leadership refused to convene the assembly. This resulted in a war in 1971 that ended in the surrender of the Pakistani forces in East Pakistan and the formation of Bangladesh as an independent country.
(ii) In 1975 Sheikh Mujib got the constitution amended to shift from the parliamentary to the presidential form of government. He also abolished all parties except his own, the Awami League. His actions were authoritarian; people opposed it, and he was assassinated in a military uprising in August 1975. The new military ruler, Ziaur Rahman, formed his own Bangladesh National Party and won elections in 1979.
(iii) Later, Ziaur Rahman was assassinated and another military takeover followed under the leadership of Lt Gen H.M. Ershad. The people of Bangladesh soon rose in support of the demand for democracy. Ershad was forced to allow political activity on a limited scale. He was later elected as President for five years. Mass public protests made Ershad step down in 1990. Elections were held in 1991. Since then representative democracy based on multi-party elections has been working in Bangladesh.
Or any other happening.

questions.text: (a) Explain the process of evolution of the European Union from an economic union to an increasingly political one.

answer.text:
Process of evolution of the European Union from an economic union to an increasingly political one (any three):
(i) European integration after 1945 was aided by the Cold War. America extended financial help under the 'Marshall Plan'.
(ii) It became a forum for Western European states to cooperate on trade and economic issues. Organisations like OEEC, Council of Europe, European Economic Community, European Parliament, and finally the European Union came up.
(iii) It also laid the foundation for a common foreign and security policy, cooperation on justice and home affairs, and the creation of a common currency.
(iv) It has also started to act more as a nation-state. The EU has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency. It also has some form of a common foreign and security policy.
(v) The EU has economic, political, democratic and military influence.
Or any other relevant points

questions.text: (b) Describe the process of evolution of the European Union from an Economic Union to an increasingly Political one.

answer.text: Evolution of the European Union from an Economic Union to an increasingly Political one (to be assessed as a whole): America extended massive financial help for reviving the European economy under the Marshall Plan. In 1948 the OEEC was established to extend cooperation on trade and economic issues among Western European states; in 1949 the Council of Europe was established for political cooperation. The process of economic integration of European capitalist countries led to the formation of the European Economic Community in 1957 — this acquired a political dimension with the creation of the European Parliament, and in 1992 the EU was formed. It also laid stress on a common foreign and security policy, cooperation on justice and home affairs, and the creation of a common currency; it started to act more as a nation state. While attempts to have a Constitution for the EU have failed, it still has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency, and some form of a common foreign and security policy in its dealings with other nations. This shows that the European Union evolved over time from an economic union to an increasingly political one.

questions.text: (a) Explain the various economic policies adopted by China that led to the rise of its economy.

answer.text:
(a) Various economic policies adopted by China that led to the rise of its economy (any four):
1. After the inception of the People's Republic of China in 1949, following the communist revolution under the leadership of Mao, its economy was based on the Soviet Model.
2. The Chinese leadership took major policy decisions in the 1970s because its industrial production was not growing fast enough, international trade was minimal and per capita income was very low.
3. China ended its political and economic isolation with the establishment of relations with the United States in 1972.
4. Premier Zhou Enlai proposed the four modernisations (agricultural, industry, science and technology, and military) in 1973.
5. In 1978, the then leader Deng Xiaoping announced the 'Open Door' policy and economic reforms in China.
6. In 1982, the privatisation of agriculture was done; in 1998, the privatisation of industry was done.
7. Trade barriers were eliminated to establish Special Economic Zones (SEZs) where foreign investors could set up enterprises.
8. In China, the state played and continues to play a central role in setting up a market economy.

questions.text: (b) Between the 1960s and the 1980s, South Korea emerged as an economic power in Asia which is termed as “Miracle on the Han River”. Explain any two reasons behind it.

answer.text:
(b) Reasons behind South Korea emerging as an economic power in Asia between the 1960s and 1980s, termed the 'Miracle on the Han River' (any two):
1. South Korea became a member of the OECD in 1996.
2. In 2017, its economy was the 11th largest in the world and its military expenditure was the 10th largest.

answer.text: Circumstances that led to the Bangladesh War in 1971: (i) The people of this region resented the domination of West Pakistan and the imposition of the Urdu language. (ii) Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman led the popular struggle against West Pakistani domination and demanded autonomy for the eastern region. (iii) In the 1970 elections, the Awami League led by Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman won all the seats in East Pakistan and secured a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly for the whole of Pakistan, but the West Pakistan leadership refused to convene the assembly. (iv) Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman was arrested and the Pakistan army under Yahya Khan tried to suppress the mass movement of the Bengali people, leading to large-scale migration into India; this created a huge refugee problem in India. The government of India supported the demand of the people of East Pakistan for independence and gave financial and military help. This resulted in a war between India and Pakistan in December 1971 that ended in the surrender of Pakistan forces in East Pakistan, which led to the formation of Bangladesh as an independent nation.

1. In 1990, the King accepted the demand for a new democratic constitution.

questions.text: (a) Explain the composition and one function of any three organs of the United Nations.

answer.text:
(i) General Assembly: It represents all 193 member states, each with one vote. Major decisions require a two-thirds majority, otherwise a simple majority decision, not binding on UN members. Key functions include adopting the UN budget, appointing the secretary general, electing non-permanent Security Council members etc.
(ii) Security Council: It has a total of 15 members, 5 permanent and 10 temporary. Permanent members are US, UK, France, Russia and China, and all these have veto power. Temporary members are elected for a term of two years. Its decisions are binding on all UN members. Key functions include investigating disputes, establishing peace and authorising military action to resolve threats to peace.
(iii) International Court of Justice: There are a total of 15 judges elected for 9 years by absolute majority in both the General Assembly and the Security Council. It is situated in 'The Hague', Netherlands. Key functions include settling legal disputes and providing advisory opinions on legal questions. It interprets and enforces international laws.
(iv) Secretariat: It acts as the UN's executive administrative arm. It is headed by the secretary-general who is appointed by the General Assembly for 5 years. It handles day-to-day work, implementing decisions, organising conferences etc.
(v) Economic and Social Council: It has 54 seats based on geographical representation which are elected by the General Assembly for three-year terms. It coordinates economic, social and environmental policies and promotes sustainable development etc.
(any three with one function)

(iii) Military actions also endanger the lives of ordinary citizens.
(iv) It is also concerned with internal security; it may be threatened by civil war and internal separatist movements.
Non-traditional notion of security:
(i) It includes a wide range of threats and dangers affecting the conditions of human existence.
(ii) The main proponents of non-traditional security are not just the state but also individuals, communities, or all of humankind.
(iii) Threats may be such as terrorism, human rights, global poverty and migration, etc.

questions.text: (b) “The non-traditional notions of security are more comprehensive than the traditional notions of security.” Support the statement with the help of suitable examples.

answer.text:
Non-Traditional notions of security go beyond military threats to include a wide range of threats and dangers affecting the conditions of human existence.
These begin by questioning the traditional referent of security. In doing so, they also question the other three elements of security — what is being secured, from what kind of threats and the approach to security.
In the traditional security conception, the referent is the state with its territory and governing institutions. In the non-traditional conceptions, the referent is expanded. According to proponents of non-traditional security, not just the state but also individuals or communities or indeed all of humankind.
Non-traditional views of security have been called human security or global security.
Non-traditional notion deals with all the contemporary threats like: (i) Global Poverty (ii) Epidemics (iii) Terrorism (iv) Environmental degradation (v) Human rights violation.
Whereas traditional security is related to the thoughts of war and military action — external or internal both.
(or any other relevant point) (Any three to be explained)

All the above sources of threat which relate to non-traditional security threats are also threats to human security. Hence the non-traditional notion of security is more or less related to human security.

(vi) It has led to the flow of ideas across national boundaries, e.g. the spread of the internet and computer-related services. (vii) It has encouraged avenues for jobs and the flow of people. (ix) Some economists have described economic globalisation as recolonisation of the world. (x) Advocates of globalisation believe it generates greater economic growth and wellbeing for larger sections of the population due to deregulation, as greater trade among countries allows each economy to do what it does best. questions.text: (a) Describe any three major challenges that independent India faced immediately after independence.

answer.text: Major challenges independent India faced immediately after independence (any three): (i) To shape a nation that was united yet accommodative of the diversity of the country — the partition appeared to prove everyone's worst fear, raising serious questions about whether India would survive as a unified country and how integration of its territory was to be achieved. (ii) The second challenge was to establish democracy — India adopted representative democracy based on the parliamentary form of government, and the challenge was to develop democratic practices in accordance with the Constitution. (iii) Another challenge was to ensure the development and well-being of the entire society and not only of some sections, based on the principle of equality and special protection to socially disadvantaged groups and religious and cultural communities.

questions.text: (b) Describe the role played by Mahatma Gandhi to reduce communal violence that erupted in many parts of India at the time of the partition in 1947.

answer.text: Role played by Mahatma Gandhi to reduce communal violence at the time of partition: Mahatma Gandhi did not participate in any of the Independence Day celebrations because of the riots and violence between Hindus and Muslims. Gandhiji's principle of Satya and Ahimsa failed to bind the people in troubled times, so his presence in Calcutta greatly improved the situation, and Independence Day in Calcutta was celebrated in a spirit of communal harmony. As the communal harmony was short-lived, riots between Hindus and Muslims erupted again, and Gandhiji had to resort to a fast to bring peace. Since large-scale violence had erupted in Delhi also, Gandhiji shifted to Delhi; various factors and policies of the government made him sad and depressed, so once again he went on a fast which proved to be his last, in January 1948 — but the effect was dramatic, communal tension and violence reduced and Muslims could now safely return to their homes. Although some people did not like Gandhiji's actions, he continued to meet everyone during his prayer meetings and continued his struggle for non-violence, justice and tolerance. (To be assessed as a whole)

questions.text: (a) Describe the difficulties faced by India to get the merger of all the Princely States into the Union of India.

answer.text: Difficulties faced by India to get the merger of all the Princely States into the Union of India (any three): Just before independence, it was announced by the British that with the end of their rule over India, the paramountcy of the British Crown over Princely States would also lapse — this meant that all these states, as many as 565 in all, would become legally independent and were free to join either India or Pakistan or remain independent if they so wished; this was a very serious problem and could threaten the very existence of a united India. The rulers of Travancore, Hyderabad and some other states had decided to remain independent. The people of most of the Princely States wanted to become a part of the Indian Union. The government was prepared to be more flexible and give autonomy to some regions. In the backdrop of partition, the integration and consolidation of territorial boundaries of the nation had assumed supreme importance.

questions.text: (b) Describe the events that led to the accession of Hyderabad into the Union of India.

answer.text: Events that led to the accession of Hyderabad into the Union of India: The Nizam of Hyderabad wanted an independent status for Hyderabad. He entered into a standstill agreement with India in November 1947. Meanwhile a people's movement against the Nizam's rule gathered force, with the communists and the Hyderabad Congress in the forefront. The Nizam unleashed the Razakars on the people — they murdered, looted, raped and maimed, particularly targeting non-Muslims. The central government ordered the army to tackle the situation, and in September 1948 the Indian Army moved in and took control of the Nizam's forces. After a few days of intermittent fighting, the Nizam surrendered, and this led to the accession of Hyderabad to India. (Assess as a whole)

questions.text: (a) Describe any three major challenges faced by India at the time of independence in 1947.

answer.text: Major challenges faced by India at the time of independence in 1947 (to be explained, any three): (i) To shape a nation that is united yet accommodative of the diversity of society. (ii) To establish and deepen democracy by ensuring fundamental rights, based on representative democracy and the parliamentary form of government. (iii) To ensure the development and well-being of the entire society.

questions.text: (b) Describe any three major difficulties that came in the way of the partition of British India in 1947.

answer.text: Major difficulties that came in the way of the partition of British India in 1947 (any three, to be explained): (i) There was no single belt of Muslim majority. (ii) All Muslims did not want to be in Pakistan. (iii) Non-Muslims were also present in large numbers in the two Muslim-majority provinces of Punjab and Bengal. (iv) Minorities on both sides found themselves trapped.

questions.text: (a) Describe any four consequences of the partition of British India in 1947.

answer.text: Consequences of the partition of British India in 1947 (any four): (i) The year 1947 was the year of one of the largest, most abrupt, unplanned and tragic transfers of population that human history has known. (ii) There were killings and atrocities on both sides of the border. (iii) Cities like Lahore, Amritsar and Kolkata became 'communal zones'. (iv) Minorities on both sides secured temporary shelter in 'refugee camps'. (v) Women were abducted, made to convert to the religion of the abductor, and were forced into marriage. (vi) In many cases, women were killed by their own family members to preserve the 'family honour'. (vii) Children were separated from their parents or orphaned. (viii) Financial assets and items like tables, chairs, typewriters, paper-clips, books and even musical instruments of the police band were divided. (ix) Employees of the government and railways were also 'divided'. (x) The ideal of a secular nation was enshrined in the Indian Constitution.

questions.text: (b) Describe any three problems that were faced during the process of partition of British India.

answer.text: Problems faced during the process of partition of British India (any three, to be explained): The principle of religious majority was to be followed for the partition of India. (i) There was no single belt of Muslim-majority area in British India. (ii) Not all Muslim-majority areas wanted to be in Pakistan. (iii) The partition of Punjab and Bengal caused the deepest trauma of partition. (iv) The problem of 'minorities' on both sides of the border made them easy targets of attack.

questions.text: (b) Describe the circumstances and events that led to Manipur's accession to India in 1949.

answer.text:
(b) Circumstances and events that led to Manipur's accession to India in 1949:
Circumstances:
1. A few days before independence, the Maharaja of Manipur, Bodhachandra Singh, signed the Instrument of Accession with the Indian government on the assurance that the internal autonomy of Manipur would be maintained.
2. Under the pressure of public opinion, the Maharaja held elections in Manipur in June 1948 and the state became a constitutional monarchy.
3. In the Legislative Assembly of Manipur there were sharp differences over the question of merger of Manipur with India.
Events:
1. While the state Congress wanted the merger, other political parties were opposed to this.
2. The Government of India succeeded in pressurising the Maharaja into signing a Merger Agreement in September 1949, without consulting the popularly elected Legislative Assembly of Manipur.
3. This caused a lot of anger and resentment in Manipur, the repercussions of which are still being felt.

questions.text: (a) Explain any two reasons responsible for the establishment of the States Reorganization Commission and highlight the basis on which new states were created.

answer.text:
(a) Two reasons responsible for the establishment of the States Reorganisation Commission, and the basis on which new states were created:
Reasons:
1. After getting independence, the challenge was to draw the internal boundaries of the Indian states; the boundaries had to be drawn so that the linguistic and cultural plurality of the country could be reflected without affecting the unity of the nation.
2. During colonial rule, the state boundaries were drawn either on administrative convenience or simply coincided with the territories annexed by the British government or the territories ruled by the princely powers, but these divisions were rejected by our national movement; after the Nagpur Session of Congress in 1920, the principle was recognised as the basis of the reorganisation of the Indian National Congress party itself.
Basis of the formation of new states:
Things changed after independence and partition; our leaders felt that carving out states on the basis of language might lead to disruption and disintegration. But at a local level, protests began in the Telugu speaking areas of the old Madras province. The movement gathered momentum as a result of the central government's vacillation. Potti Sriramulu, a Congress leader and a veteran Gandhian, went on an indefinite fast that led to his death after 56 days. This caused great unrest and resulted in violent outbursts in the Andhra region. Consequently, the Prime Minister announced the formation of a separate Andhra State in December 1952. Due to the above reasons, the State Reorganisation Commission was set up in 1953.

questions.text: (b) Analyse any three reasons for the declaration of Emergency in 1975.

answer.text:
Reasons for declaring Emergency in 1975 (any three):
(i) Tensions in the relationship between the government and the judiciary. The Congress advocated parliamentary supremacy and alleged the judiciary was a conservative institution.
(ii) After the Bangladesh war, prices were rising and expectations of the people were raised by the slogan 'Garibi Hatao'. People were unsatisfied and agitated when these were not fulfilled.
(iii) The Gujarat and Bihar movements - student unrest and participation of leaders like Morarji Desai and Jayaprakash Narayan put the government into trouble.
(iv) The judgement of the Allahabad High Court on 12th June 1975, which declared the election of Indira Gandhi (PM) invalid. Accordingly, she was no longer a member of the Lok Sabha, which was a threat to her Prime Ministership.
(v) Combined opposition parties demanded her resignation - the Ramlila Maidan rally, where JP gave a call and asked the army, the police and government employees not to obey illegal and immoral orders. All these reasons combined together led to the declaration of Emergency.

questions.text: (a) How is ‘one party dominance’ in India different from the ‘one party dominance system’ of other countries ? Analyse with the help of examples.

answer.text:
India is not the only country that has experienced the dominance of one party. Many other examples exist of one-party dominance, but there is a crucial difference between these and the Indian experience. In other countries, dominance of one party was ensured by compromising democracy:
(i) In some countries like China, Cuba and Syria, the Constitution permits only a single party to rule the country. But in India, the Constitution does not mention any provision regarding a one-party system.
(ii) In some countries like Myanmar, Belarus, Egypt and Eritrea, effectively one-party dominant states exist due to legal and military measures. But India is a democratic country with a multi-party system.
(iii) Until a few years ago, Mexico, South Korea and Taiwan were also effectively one-party dominance states. But in India, one-party dominance is under democratic conditions. In India, many parties have contested elections under conditions of free and fair elections, and yet the Congress managed to win election after election.

questions.text: (b) Analyse the various aspects of the Presidential election of 1969, which led to the formal split in the Congress Party.

answer.text:
Various aspects of the Presidential election of 1969, which led to the formal split in the Congress Party:
(i) Despite Indira Gandhi's resentment, the Syndicate nominated N. Sanjeeva Reddy as the official Congress candidate for the presidential elections.
(ii) Indira Gandhi retaliated by encouraging V.V. Giri, the then Vice President, to be nominated as an independent candidate.
(iii) During the elections, the then Congress President S. Nijalingappa issued a 'whip', asking all Congress MPs and MLAs to vote for N. Sanjeeva Reddy.
(iv) On the other hand, PM Indira Gandhi openly called for a conscience vote, to vote the way they wanted.
(v) The elections went in favour of V.V. Giri, and the defeat of N. Sanjeeva Reddy formalized the split of the Congress party into two: Congress (O) and Congress (R).

answer.text: India's general elections of 1952 became a landmark in the history of democracy all over the world because: due to the size of the Indian electorate and the country, the election was unusual — no election on this scale had ever been conducted in the world before. To prepare the electoral rolls, the list of all citizens eligible to vote was a challenging task. Moreover, it was the first big test of democracy in a poor and illiterate country with narrow loyalties in terms of caste, religion, language etc. It was an experiment of universal adult franchise at a very large scale in the world. Preparation for the election was a mammoth exercise but done successfully — over one lakh officers were trained for polling and the effort made was successful. More than 50% of voters used their votes, which silenced critics all over the world regarding this grand achievement, a landmark in history. (Evaluate as a whole)

questions.text: (b) Explain any three important features of India's Nuclear Policy.

questions.text: (a) Describe the role of Jaya Prakash Narayan in Indian National Politics.

answer.text:
(a) Role of Jaya Prakash Narayan in Indian National Politics:
1. He led the Bihar movement in 1974, when Bihar students invited him to lead.
2. He accepted the invitation on the condition that the movement should be non-violent and not be limited only to Bihar territory.
3. On his appeal, people from all walks of life joined the movement.
4. He demanded the dismissal of the Congress Government in Bihar and gave a call for total revolution.
5. In 1975, J.P. Narayan led a people's march to the Parliament, one of the largest political rallies ever held in the capital.
6. He opposed the emergency and became the symbol of restoration of democracy.
7. He was supported by most of the non-Congress opposition parties.
Or any other relevant point (assess as a whole).

4. The Janata Party highlighted various excesses such as preventive detention and press censorship, to get favourable public opinion.
5. Janata Party was a coalition of opposition parties; it ensured that non-Congress votes were not divided.
6. Middle class people of North India were moving away from Congress and Janata Party became a platform for them.
Or any other relevant reason.

questions.text: Explain any four effects of the Emergency declared in 1975.

answer.text:
Effects of the Emergency declared in 1975 (any four):
(i) Thousands of people and leaders were arrested under the Preventive Detention Act.
(ii) The Parliament brought in many changes in the Constitution; for example, an amendment declaring that elections of the Prime Minister, President and Vice-President were non-justiciable was made.
(iii) Political parties of the opposition joined hands to form a new party, the 'Janata Party'.
(iv) People became more aware about their Fundamental Rights and liberty.
(v) People became aware about the freedom of the press.
Or any other relevant effect

questions.text: (a) Assess any three effects of Emergency imposed in 1975 in strengthening the democracy in India.

answer.text:
Effects of Emergency imposed in 1975 in strengthening democracy in India (any three):
(i) Democracy in India was strengthened.
(ii) People became aware about their rights and the importance of liberty.
(iii) People also realised the importance of the 'Freedom of Press'.
(iv) People understood the value of their 'Voting Rights' and used the right to get the government of their choice.
(v) People did not become violent against the Emergency but waited for the right moment to use their democratic rights.
(vi) The elections in 1977 were a silent revolution against the excesses, but in favour of democracy.
Or any other relevant point

questions.text: (b) Assess the impact of three democratic upsurges in post independent India.

answer.text:
Impact of three democratic upsurges in post-independent India:
(i) The First Democratic Upsurge is attributed to the 1950s-1970s, based on the participation of Indian adult voters in democratic politics both at the centre and in the states, falsifying the western myth that the success of democracy requires modernization, urbanization, education and access to media.
(ii) During the 1980s, the increasing political participation of the lower classes of society, such as SCs, STs and OBCs, has been interpreted as the 'Second Democratic Upsurge'.
(iii) The Third Democratic Upsurge represents a competitive electoral market, based not on the principle of survival of the fittest but rather the survival of the ablest. It underlines three shifts in India's electoral market: from State to Market, from Government to Governance, from State as Controller to State as Facilitator. It seeks to promote the participation of the youth. This upsurge is attributed to the 1990s.

questions.text: Why is the period around Emergency of 1975 known as the period of constitutional crisis ? Highlight any one reason.

The period around the Emergency of 1975 is known as a period of constitutional crisis, focused on (any one):

(ii) Whether Parliament could curtail the right to property.
(iii) The Parliament amended the Constitution saying it could abridge Fundamental Rights to give effect to Directive Principles, but the Supreme Court rejected it.
(iv) In June 1975, the election of Indira Gandhi as MP was declared null and void by the Allahabad High Court, but after her appeal in the Supreme Court she could remain an MP but could not take part in the proceedings of the Lok Sabha.
(v) There was no coordination among the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary.

questions.text: (a) Why is the emergency imposed in 1975 considered the most controversial episode in Indian politics ? Highlight any three reasons.

answer.text:
Reasons why the Emergency imposed in 1975 is considered the most controversial episode in Indian politics (any three):
(i) Democracy was negated for the first time.
(ii) Fundamental Rights were openly violated.
(iii) Freedom of the press was curtailed.
(iv) Misuse of the preventive detention law.
(v) Excesses were committed all over the country, e.g. custodial deaths.
(vi) Abuse of authority - exercise of governmental power by people who held no official position, for example demolitions and forced sterilization in Delhi became very controversial.
(vii) Controversy over Parliament's power to amend basic features of the Constitution.
(viii) Political controversy regarding superseding of three judges to the Supreme Court.
Or any other relevant points

questions.text: (b) Highlight any three factors which were responsible for the downfall of the Congress Party in the 1977 elections.

answer.text:
Factors responsible for the downfall of the Congress Party in the 1977 elections (any three):
(i) The Emergency imposed in 1975 - the 1977 elections turned into a referendum on the experience of Emergency.
(ii) The experience of the Emergency brought forth that governments perceived to be anti-democratic are severely punished by the voters.
(iii) Unification of the opposition parties against Congress; formation of the Janata Party, to ensure that non-Congress votes would not be divided.
(iv) Some leaders of the Congress were also opposed to the Emergency; they joined the new party.
(v) The Janata Party made this election into a referendum on the Emergency.
(vi) The opposition fought the election on the slogan 'Save Democracy'.
(vii) The Janata Party focused its campaign on the non-democratic character of the rule and on the various excesses that took place during this period.
(viii) In the backdrop of the arrests of thousands of persons and censorship of the press, public opinion was against the Congress.
(ix) Jaya Prakash Narayan became the popular symbol of the restoration of democracy.
Any other relevant points

questions.text: (a) Highlight any two lessons learnt from the imposition of Emergency in India in 1975.

answer.text: Lessons learnt from the imposition of Emergency in 1975 (brief explanation of any two): (i) It is extremely difficult to do away with democracy in India. (ii) It brought some ambiguities regarding certain emergency provisions in the constitution that have since been rectified. (iii) The Emergency made everyone more aware of the value of civil liberties. (iv) There is a need to maintain a balance between the functioning of a democratic government and continuous political protest by parties and groups. (v) Institutions like the police and the administration can be turned into political instruments of the ruling party. Or any other relevant point.

questions.text: (b) Highlight any four consequences of the imposition of Emergency in India in 1975.

answer.text: Consequences of the imposition of Emergency in 1975 (any four): (i) It brought the agitation to an abrupt stop; strikes were banned; many opposition leaders were put in jail; the political situation became very quiet though tense. (ii) The government suspended freedom of the press — newspapers were asked to get prior approval for all material to be published, known as press censorship. (iii) Apprehending social and communal disharmony, the government banned the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and Jamaat-e-Islami. (iv) Various Fundamental Rights of citizens were suspended, including the right to move the court for restoring Fundamental Rights. (v) Using the Preventive Detention Act, the government made large-scale arrests. (vi) In support of the government, the doors of the courts were closed to citizens. (vii) Many writers returned their National Awards such as Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri, in protest against the suspension of democracy. (viii) The parliament made many amendments to the constitution. Or any other relevant point.

answer.text: The best way to respond to regional aspirations is through democratic negotiations. For example, during the 1980s, militancy had erupted in Punjab; there were problems in the North-East; students in Assam were agitating and the Kashmir Valley was boiling. Instead of treating these issues with simple law and order measures, the Government of India negotiated settlements with regional movements — this produced reconciliation (through the Punjab Accord, Assam Accord, etc.) that reduced tensions existing in many states. questions.text: Describe the events that took place in Sikkim from the time of India’s independence to its merger with India.

answer.text: Events that took place in Sikkim from independence to its merger with India (to be assessed as a whole): At the time of independence, Sikkim was a 'protectorate' of India and not a fully sovereign country. It was not a part of India — Sikkim's defence and relations were looked after by India, while internal administration was with the Chogyal, Sikkim's monarch. The first democratic election in Sikkim was held in 1974, and the Sikkim Congress swept the elections. The Sikkim Assembly passed a resolution in 1975 asking for integration with India, followed by a referendum that stamped popular approval; the Indian Parliament immediately accepted it, and Sikkim became the 22nd state of the Indian Union.

questions.text: “Regionalism is not as dangerous as communalism.” Justify the statement.

Or any other relevant point.

questions.text: (a) “Regional demands from different parts of India show that India has adopted a democratic approach to accommodate diversity.” Justify the statement.

answer.text:
(a) "Regional demands from different parts of India show that India has adopted a democratic approach to accommodate diversity":
1. India's democratic politics allows people and groups to address the people on the basis of their regional identity, aspirations and specific regional problems.
2. India's democratic politics focuses on regional issues and problems to receive adequate attention and accommodation in the policy-making process, i.e. regional aspirations of Assam, Punjab, North-East, Kashmir, etc.
3. Examples: in the eighties, militancy erupted in Punjab, problems persisted in the North-East, students agitated in Assam, and the Kashmir valley was on the boil.
4. The government of India settled many regional issues through negotiations to reduce tensions in many regions.
5. Mizoram is an example of a political settlement to resolve the problem of separation effectively.
(Evaluate as a whole)

questions.text: (a) Analyse any three reasons for the movement against outsiders in Assam from 1979 to 1985.

answer.text:
(a) Reasons for the movement against outsiders in Assam from 1979 to 1985 (any three):
1. The Assamese suspected that there were a huge number of illegal Bengali Muslim settlers from Bangladesh.
2. They suspected that these outsiders would reduce the indigenous Assamese into a minority.
3. The outsiders are held responsible for the exploitation of natural resources; these outsiders would drain out the natural resources of the state without any benefit to the local population.
4. Assamese people also found the impact of outsiders on their culture.
Or any other relevant point.

questions.text: (b) Analyse any three reasons for the unrest and violence in Punjab from 1967 to 1985.

answer.text:
(b) Reasons for the unrest and violence in Punjab from 1967 to 1985 (any three):
1. Akalis formed the government in 1967 and 1977; on both occasions it was a coalition government that was dismissed by the Union Government.
2. They did not enjoy strong support among Hindus.
3. The Anandpur Sahib resolution was passed in 1973, which was for autonomy and wanted to redefine centre-state relationships; the resolution spoke of the aspirations of the Sikh community and declared its goal as attaining the dominance of Sikhs.
4. Operation Blue Star led to large-scale violence.
5. Assassination of Indira Gandhi also sparked violence.
Or any other relevant point.

questions.text: (a) Assess the reasons for the Dravidian Movement and its outcomes.

answer.text:
(a) Reasons for the Dravidian Movement and its outcomes:
This movement was led by the Tamil social reformer E.V. Ramasamy 'Periyar'. This movement strongly opposed the Brahmins' dominance and affirmed regional pride against the political, economic and cultural domination of the North.
Political implications: It led to the formation of the Dravidar Kazhagam (DK). Later on, the DK split and the political legacy of the movement was transferred to the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK). The DMK made its entry into politics with a three-pronged agitation in 1953-54.
Outcomes:
1. Initially, it spoke in terms of the whole of South India; however, lack of support from other states limited it to only Tamil Nadu.
2. It strongly opposed the Hindi language; this may be seen even today.
Or any other relevant point.

questions.text: (a) “India has accepted expressions of regional aspirations to strengthen the national integrity.” Support the statement with two examples.

answer.text:
(i) India adopted a democratic approach regarding the expressions of regional aspirations. It did not look upon the demands of regional aspirations as anti-national. For example, states of Haryana, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were created from their parent states. Thus the expression of regional aspiration strengthens national integrity.
(ii) India allows parties and groups to address the people on the basis of their regional aspirations. For example, All Assam Students Union (AASU) in Assam and Mizo National Front (MNF) in Mizoram tried to solve their regional issues.
(iii) In India, peoples' movements in Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland were not treated as against the unity of the nation but were heard and decided on the basis of negotiation and deliberation. Democratic process was adopted in all these cases.
(or any other relevant examples) (any two)

questions.text: How does the geographical location of the North-East region has affected the expression of its regional demands ? Explain.

answer.text:
(i) The geographical isolation of the region, its complex social character and its backwardness compared to the other parts of the country have resulted in the complicated sets of demands for different states of North East.
(ii) North-Eastern region has only four percent of the country's population but about twice as much share of its area. A small corridor of about 22 km connects the region to the rest of the country and makes it important geographically.
(iii) The partition of India reduced the North-East to a land locked region and affected its economy which created unrest.
(iv) Cut off from the rest of India, the region suffered neglect in terms of development, demands for autonomy and separation were raised.
(v) Its politics remained insulated.
(vi) Due to migrants, major demographic changes occurred. Vast international border and weak communication between the north-east and the rest of India added to its demands for autonomy, movement for succession and opposition to outsiders.
(or any other relevant point) (any two)

questions.text: (b) Explain the main factors responsible for the demands of autonomy by the north-eastern states in India.

answer.text:
At the time of independence the entire region of North-East except Manipur and Tripura comprised the state of Assam. Factors for demand of autonomy are:
(i) The isolation of the region.
(ii) Its complex social character.
(iii) Its backwardness as compared to the other parts of the country.
(iv) Vast international border and weak communication between the North-East and the rest of India.
(v) Assam government imposed the Assamese language on non-Assamese people. Non-Assamese felt a threat from this imposition.
(vi) Communities like the Bodos, Karbis and Dimasas wanted separate states. They also worked for this demand by mobilising public opinion and popular movement as well as through insurgency.
(vii) Leaders of major tribal communities wanted separation from Assam.
(viii) Some of them formed the Eastern India Tribal Union to be carved out of Assam.
(ix) For the government of India it was not possible to form smaller states.
(x) Nagaland, Mizoram claimed that they had never been a part of the Indian union.
(or any other relevant point) (any 3 points to be explained)

questions.text: (b) Describe any three measures that can be taken by the Union government to address the regional movements and demands.

answer.text:
(i) The Indian government's approach considers regional aspirations to be very much a part of democracy.
(ii) The best way to respond to regional aspirations is through democratic negotiations rather than separation.
(iii) To respect the process of power sharing.
(iv) India addresses regional economic development in a balanced manner.
(v) The Indian approach is to accommodate diversity and to build a strong nation.
(vi) The demands of different regions and political parties help the central government to know and assess the aspirations of the people.
(or any other relevant point) (Any three)

questions.text: (a) ‘Regional aspirations and demands are part and parcel of democratic politics.’ Support the statement with three examples.

answer.text:
Regional aspirations are not against unity or the democratic process. Expression of regional aspirations and demands leads the government to think about the issue raised and to take steps to solve or fulfil the demands. For example:
(i) Movements in Nagaland and Manipur led the government to address their problems and demands. Negotiations were initiated and efforts were made towards resolution.
(ii) The movement in Punjab before 1966 resulted in the creation of a Punjabi-speaking state, and later dissatisfaction was reduced through the Punjab Accord.
(iii) The movement against outsiders in Assam was resolved through negotiations with AASU in 1985, leading to satisfaction among a large section of the population.
(Any other relevant point) (Three points to be explained)

questions.text: (b) Suggest any three measures to strengthen ‘unity in diversity’ in India.

answer.text:
(i) The government should avoid suppressing movements through harsh measures and instead adopt a democratic approach.
(ii) It should carefully consider the demands and aspirations of the people and promote dialogue with regional leaders to arrive at a mutually acceptable solution.
(iii) The Union government should ensure balanced regional development so that all states and regions receive their due share.
(iv) It should respect cultural and linguistic diversity and refrain from imposing any particular language or culture on any region.
(v) Interaction and visits by Union leaders should aim at understanding the concerns and aspirations of different regions.
(vi) The federal structure of India should be upheld and respected in both spirit and practice.
(Any other relevant point) (Three points to be explained)

questions.text: (a) Highlight any three major developments that took place in Indian politics during NDA III and NDA IV.

answer.text:
Major developments that took place in Indian politics during NDA III and NDA IV (any three):

The NDA III coalition was dominated by BJP with an absolute majority of its own in the Lok Sabha, and was referred to as a 'surplus majority coalition'.
(ii) The 2019 Lok Sabha elections once again brought back the BJP-led NDA IV to the Centre. The BJP on its own won 303 seats in the Lok Sabha, the biggest number any single party has won in the lower house since 1984.
(iii) A shift from caste- and religion-based politics to development- and good governance-oriented politics.
(iv) Several socio-economic welfare schemes have been initiated to make development and governance accessible to the masses, such as Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, Jan Dhan Yojana, Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana, Kisan Fasal Bima Yojana, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, Ayushman Bharat, etc.

questions.text: (a) How are the three recommendations of the Mandal Commission an effort to solve the problems of the ‘Other Backward Classes’ (OBCs) ? Analyse.

answer.text:
How the three recommendations of the Mandal Commission were an effort to solve the problems of the Other Backward Classes (OBCs) - analysis (any three):
(i) Reservation of 27% of seats in educational institutions helped enhance the opportunities of OBCs to get higher education.
(ii) 27% of seats were reserved in government jobs, which provided extra opportunities to the youth of OBCs to get employment and lead a respectful life.
(iii) The Mandal Commission recommended land reforms to improve the living conditions of the OBCs.
(iv) The Commission advised that 'backward classes' should be understood to mean 'backward castes', since many castes, other than Scheduled Castes, were also treated as low in the caste hierarchy.
(v) The National Front government decided to implement one of the recommendations of the Mandal Commission pertaining to reservations for OBCs in jobs in the central government and its undertakings.

questions.text: (a) Explain any three major developments which took place in Indian politics during the last decade of the 20th century.

answer.text: Major developments in Indian politics during the last decade of the 20th century (any three): (i) Decline of the Congress System — the defeat of the Congress Party in the 1989 election marked the end of Congress dominance over the Indian party system; it could win only 197 seats in the Lok Sabha. (ii) Rise of the Mandal Issue — this started with the National Front Government's decision to implement the recommendation of the Mandal Commission that jobs in the Central government should be reserved for OBCs, leading to violent anti-Mandal protests in different parts of the country. (iii) New Economic Policy — the government adopted the New Economic Policy in 1991, started under Rajiv Gandhi; these changes first became visible in 1991 and radically changed the direction the Indian economy had pursued since independence. (iv) Demolition of the Babri Masjid / Ayodhya dispute — the Ayodhya dispute intensified with the demolition of the disputed structure at Ayodhya in December 1992, leading to various changes in the politics of the country and raising questions about the nature of Indian nationalism and secularism. (v) Assassination of Rajiv Gandhi — his assassination in May 1991 led to a change in Congress leadership; in the 1991 election Congress emerged as the single largest party and P.V. Narasimha Rao was elected Prime Minister of India.

questions.text: (b) In the midst of severe competition and many conflicts after 1989, a consensus appeared to have emerged among most parties. Explain any three points of consensus.

answer.text: Points of consensus that emerged among most parties after 1989 despite severe competition (any three): (i) Agreement on new economic policies — most parties supported the new economic policies and believed they would lead the country to prosperity and a status of economic power in the world. (ii) Acceptance of the political and social claims of the backward castes — political parties recognised that the social and political claims of the backward castes needed to be accepted and supported reservation of seats for OBCs in education and employment. (iii) Acceptance of the role of state-level parties in governance of the country — state-level parties shared power at the national level and played a central role in the country's politics. (iv) Emphasis on pragmatic considerations rather than ideological positions — political alliances formed without ideological agreement, as most parties of the NDA did not agree with the 'Hindutva' ideology of the BJP, yet came together to form a government and remained in power for a full term.
